title: Synchronous Thermochromic and Heat-Response-Enhanced Anisotropic Conductive Janus Film Functionalized by Upconverting Luminescence for Multi-Scenario Applications
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Developing stimulus-responsive multifunctional materials for multi-scenarios is meaningful. Herein, synchronous thermochromic and heat-response-enhanced anisotropic conductive Janus films (STHACJFs) are first designed and fabricated by respectively utilizing Janus-nanofiber and composite-nanofiber as microscopic building units to form the down-layer heat-response-enhanced anisotropic conductive Janus-nanofibers array membranes (HACJAMs) and up-layer thermochromic composite-nanofibers array membranes (TCAMs) of Janus films via electrospinning. Thermochromic transition temperatures of TCAMs are innovatively designed to match with response temperatures of HACJAMs, thereby enabling synchronous thermochromism and conductive anisotropy enhancement under single-temperature stimulation. The Janus-nanofiber with two micro-partitions endows HACJAMs with high conductive anisotropy and strong luminescence. An innovative strategy combining the phase transition-enhanced conductivity of W-doped VO2 with the intrinsic conductivity of polyaniline (PANI) is proposed to enhance the conductive anisotropy degree upon heating, and response temperatures of HACJAMs are regulated by adjusting W atomic percentages to tune the phase transition temperatures of W-doped VO2. Upon heating to 60, 55, and 45 °C, W-doped VO2 and PANI synergistically enhance the conductivity along the length direction of Janus-nanofiber, and the introduction of Na3ZrF7: Yb3+, Er3+ endows intense insulating capability in the diameter direction, realizing a heat-response-enhanced anisotropic conduction (ca. 105) in HACJAMs, while TCAMs exhibit distinct color transitions from pink, blue, and green to white at these temperatures, respectively. Both HACJAMs and TCAMs exhibit red upconverting luminescence under 980 nm laser excitation. By virtue of their superior multifunctionality, STHACJFs enable low-voltage electrical interconnection and dual-mode temperature indication in multi-temperature scenarios in a newly designed transistor switch circuit. Furthermore, STHACJFs demonstrate various applications, including transient thermal printing, temperature monitoring, static and dynamic anti-counterfeiting, temperature-controlled password recognition, and multilevel and multimodal information encryption. This research advances new anisotropic conductive membranes and stimulus-responsive multifunctional nanostructured materials.

title: Revealing Decomposition Pathways of an Ethylene Carbonate-Based Electrolyte with Fiber-Optic FTIR in NCM811 Li-Ion Cells
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Ni-rich NCM811 cathode is critical for achieving high-energy-density lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) but its instability issue at high potentials vs Li/Li+ remains unresolved. Mechanical degradation and lattice oxygen release of NCM811 could trigger nonequilibrium interfacial side reactions, including electrolyte oxidation, interphase evolution, and impedance growth. Understanding these processes is essential for the rational design of stable high-voltage electrolytes compatible with NCM811 cathodes. Here, we combine operando fiber-optic absorption mid-infrared Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy with a customized three-electrode NCM811|graphite full cell to track the evolution of an 1.5 M LiPF6/ethylene carbonate (EC) electrolyte during the formation cycles. Our analyses reveal that the EC carbonyl and PF6– -associated bands exhibit a synchronous maximum attenuation rate near 3.8 V vs Li/Li+, indicating coupled perturbation of the salt–solvent coordination environment. EC-derived ring-opening products and phosphorus-containing intermediates continue to accumulate during discharge, while reactive fluorophosphorus species undergo restructuring accompanied by the formation of oxidized carbonyl products during the subsequent constant-voltage charge. Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy further shows that the increase in cell impedance originates predominantly from the NCM811 cathode rather than the graphite anode. These findings establish an isolated electrode–electrolyte interfacial framework for understanding coupled electrolyte decomposition in Ni-rich full cells and provide mechanistic insights into electrolyte/interface engineering for high-energy-density LIBs.

title: A Dual-Crosslinked Coating with a Stable Self-generating Hydrogel Surface and Suppressed Water Permeation for Intrinsic Marine Antifouling
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract To address the challenge of simultaneously achieving optimal antifouling efficacy and service durability for hydrogel coatings, dual-crosslinkable coatings were facilely fabricated from a polyacrylate bearing three functional groups (trimethoxysilyl, triisopropylsilyl ester, and ethyl acetoacetate groups) and a blended curing agent (amino-silane and branched polyethyleneimine). Upon seawater immersion, the coatings could rapidly self-generate an underwater superoleophobic surface characterized by hydrogel or porous structures, depending on their composition. Remarkably, the optimized coating (T14K14A14/15%P) maintained its hydrogel layer at the surface during 30 d of both static and dynamic immersion tests, indicating suppressed water permeation and hydrolysis within the coating and hence outstanding durability in service. This behavior was attributed to the barrier effect of the dense dual-crosslinked networks and the osmotic potential of the salt-entrapped hydrogel layer. Although no antifouling agent was incorporated, the T14K14A14/15%P coating exhibited an initial sterilization rate above 99%, which remained above 90% after 30 d of immersion, with protein and algal adhesion reductions of 93.5 and 93.1%, respectively. Through direct immersion and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy, the coating also demonstrated decent anticorrosion performance even after long-term immersion, further verifying the suppressed water permeation. This work provides a strategy for designing durable hydrogel antifouling coatings without compromising antifouling performance.

title: Covalent Interfacial Engineering for Suppressing Defect and Phonon-Mediated Losses in Perovskite Quantum Dots/Polymer Composites
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Addressing the synergistic nonradiative losses in CsPbBr3 perovskite quantum dots (PQDs)/polymer composites arising from interfacial defects and lattice softness is crucial for enhancing the photoluminescence performance. This study proposes a molecular interface engineering strategy employing the crosslinkable ligand 2-carboxyethyl acrylate (CEA). By constructing coordination-covalent bonds and covalent interfaces between CEA-modified CsPbBr3 PQDs and a polymer matrix formed via the copolymerization of CEA and pentaerythritol triacrylate monomer, the resulting composites achieve a photoluminescence quantum yield of 78% along with enhanced water and thermal stability, retaining approximately 83% of their initial emission intensity after 15 days of water immersion and 41% emission intensity at 393 K after continuous heating. Femtosecond transient absorption and variable-temperature photoluminescence spectra reveal that the covalent interfaces not only passivate surface defects and suppress nonradiative recombination but also effectively reduce exciton-phonon coupling and multi-phonon relaxation processes by enhancing lattice rigidity and increasing optical phonon energy.

title: A Zwitterionic Polymeric Quaternary Ammonium Microparticle (Z-pQAM) as a Candidate Wound Dressing with Simultaneous Procoagulant, Antimicrobial, and Wound-Healing Activities
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Wound infection, inadequate local hemostasis, and delayed healing remain major complications following surgery and in chronic wounds. Effective wound management requires materials that simultaneously prevent infection, support hemostasis, promote tissue repair, and maintain biocompatibility. Here, we synthesized a zwitterionic polymeric quaternary ammonium microparticle (Z-pQAM) and evaluated its biocompatibility, in vitro antimicrobial and procoagulant activity, and wound-healing effects. FTIR confirmed stepwise synthesis and quaternization, and zeta potential analysis showed that Z-pQAM retains a net-negative bulk surface charge across physiological pH. In vitro degradation studies in PBS showed that Z-pQAM retained >99% of its dry mass after three weeks, indicating slow, physiologically appropriate hydrolytic degradation. Functional assays are in line with the hypothesis that its procoagulant and antibacterial activity arise from locally accessible quaternary ammonium (QA+) microdomains rather than overall surface positivity. Z-pQAM achieved >7-log10 reduction against S. aureus and E. coli, and >5-log10 reduction against MRSA at 200 mg/mL, with Live/Dead staining confirming bactericidal membrane disruption, while maintaining <0.5% hemolysis and 100% cell viability across the tested concentration range. In recalcified whole blood, Z-pQAM achieved a blood clotting index of 36.5%, comparable to a benchmark FDA-cleared hemostatic powder. In an uninfected murine full-thickness excisional wound model, topical Z-pQAM accelerated closure at day 8 without altering epidermal thickness, reduced CD45+ inflammatory infiltration by >50% at day 3, and enhanced collagen deposition by day 12. Collectively, these findings position Z-pQAM as a promising candidate for a multifunctional topical wound dressing, combining antibacterial and procoagulant activity with biocompatibility and support for wound repair.

title: GO Coating-Assisted Deformation and Failure Regulation of Glass Fibers under High-Speed Impact
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Continuous glass fiber (GF) reinforced polymers (GFRPs) are widely used in high-performance applications due to their excellent mechanical properties. A new coating strategy involving coating graphene oxide (GO) on the fibers has been shown to effectively enhance the mechanical properties and durability of their 3D printed composites. However, their performance under high-speed impact loading deserves attention. In this study, the reinforcement mechanism of GO coatings on GF substrates under high-speed bending conditions is investigated using molecular dynamics (MD) simulations. Both single-layer and bilayer GO coatings were evaluated to understand their effects on impact-induced deformation behavior and energy dissipation capacity. The results demonstrate that GO coatings significantly enhance the resistance to impact-induced deformation, resulting in increases in the perforation threshold velocity of 46.9 and 71.9% for single-layer and bilayer coatings, respectively. The presence of GO coatings introduces distinct deformation and failure behaviors, thereby enhancing energy absorption and improving resistance to impact-induced perforation. These findings offer valuable insights into optimizing GO-coated GFs for applications requiring enhanced impact resistance, such as aerospace, automotive safety, and protective components.

title: Green-Solvent-Processed Janus Membranes for Subambient Radiative Cooling and Unidirectional Sweat Transport
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Extreme heat events are escalating globally, driving an urgent need for personal thermal-wet management materials. However, existing radiative cooling textiles face a persistent trilemma, including toxic organic solvents, efficient sweat dissipation with sacrificed cooling, and end-of-life recyclability. Here, we break this trade-off by a green-solvent-processed moisture-thermal management membrane (G-MTMM) via sequential electrospinning. This membrane consists of hydrophobic polyvinyl butyral skin layer and hydrophilic alcohol-soluble nylon/Al2O3 environmental layer, creating an asymmetric wettability and pore-size gradient. This design achieves solar reflectance of 95.46% and atmospheric-window emissivity of 90.80%, driven by multiscale Mie scattering from the hierarchical network and γ-Al2O3 nanoparticles, complemented by complementary molecular vibrations of polymers and Al–O lattice phonons. Under 100 mW cm–2 simulated sunlight, G-MTMM reduces the temperature of a simulated skin by 14.9 °C compared with cotton, and outdoor tests demonstrate a subambient cooling of –3.17 °C under peak solar irradiance. The Laplace pressure difference arising from the wettability and pore-size contrast enables unidirectional liquid sweat transport from the hydrophobic skin side to the hydrophilic environment side with a one-way transport index of 734.5% and anti-gravity pumping capability. G-MTMM also exhibits excellent flexibility, mechanical durability, washability, and closed-loop recyclability, offering a novel paradigm for sustainable personal thermal-wet comfort.

title: Garnet Nanofiber Scaffolds and Sulfonated Graphene Enable Stable Li+ Transport in Polymer Electrolytes
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract The practical application of solid polymer electrolytes remains limited by sluggish Li+ transport and insufficient interfacial stability. Herein, a PVDF-HFP-based composite solid polymer electrolyte was developed by incorporating Al-doped garnet-type LLZO nanofibers (LLZAO) and sulfonated graphene (SG) as functional components into the PVDF-HFP matrix. This design creates a continuous ceramic transport scaffold and a polar interfacial network. LLZAO provides mechanical reinforcement and long-range Li+ transport pathways, whereas the sulfonic acid sites of SG promote lithium salt dissociation and regulate local Li+ coordination and anion distribution. Synchrotron X-ray tomography, synchrotron radiation Fourier transform infrared (SR-FTIR), in situ small-angle X-ray scattering (SAXS), soft X-ray absorption spectroscopy/X-ray absorption near-edge structure (sXAS/XANES), and resonant inelastic X-ray scattering (RIXS) further reveal that the three-dimensionally interconnected LLZAO fiber scaffold establishes a continuous Li+ transport network. Meanwhile, the polar sites of SG enhance lithium salt dissociation and regulate interfacial coordination. Together, these components stabilize the nanoscale multiphase structure during cycling. The resulting electrolyte exhibits an ionic conductivity of 4.6 × 10–4 S cm–1 at 60 °C. This work provides a new strategy for the synergistic construction of continuous ion-transport pathways and stable coordination interfaces in composite polymer electrolytes.

title: Fluorination‑driven σ‑bonding design enables practical aqueous zinc-vanadium‑oxide batteries
source: Physical sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Vanadium-based positive electrodes for aqueous batteries offer high-capacity, low-cost energy storage but are limited by vanadium dissolution and sluggish kinetics. Amorphization alleviates kinetic limitations by creating open ion-transport pathways, yet vanadium dissolution remains unresolved. Here, we propose a coordination-engineering strategy that stabilizes amorphous vanadium oxides via fluorine incorporation, thereby suppressing vanadium dissolution without compromising fast ion-transport kinetics. Replacing O2- with highly electronegative F- converts labile σ + π V-O coordination into robust σ-dominated V-F coordination. The resulting V-F bonding weakens interactions with H2O and suppresses water-induced degradation, whereas the comparable ionic radii of F- and O2- allow substitution without perturbing amorphous framework, preserving fast ion transport. Consequently, aqueous zinc-ion batteries assembled with the fluorinated amorphous vanadium oxide positive electrode exhibit fast kinetics and long-term cycling stability, delivering a high specific capacity of 155.6 mAh g−1 at 200 A g−1, stable cycling for up to 70,000 cycles at 100 A g−1, and durable operation at 0.1 A g−1 (20 mg cm−2) for over six months. This work shows that fluorine-induced reconstruction of the local coordination environment can resolve the stability-kinetics trade-off in amorphous electrodes, providing a microscopic-to-macroscopic design principle for aqueous batteries.

title: Mesophase-induced vitrification in coordination polymers via aliphatic chain dynamics
source: Physical sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Hybrid glasses of coordination polymers promise a fusion of processability and structural functionality, yet their formation is limited by poor thermal stability and high melting points. Here, we show mesophase-induced vitrification in a series of magnesium-based coordination polymers with aliphatic dicarboxylate linkers of varying chain length. Upon thermal desolvation, these frameworks transition into a mesomorphic state that retains the long-range order of the parent framework while disordering the organic substructure. This intermediate state enables a direct glass transition without melting. In contrast, only the longest-chain analogue melts, and its melt-quenched glass has lower stiffness owing to partial dissociation of the metal–organic backbone, indicating that mechanical properties are governed by the integrity of the coordination network. Spectroscopic and structural analyses show that vitrification proceeds through mobilisation of the aliphatic linker within an intact coordination network, paralleling semicrystalline polymers. These findings establish a design strategy for vitrifiable coordination networks that integrates principles from polymer dynamics and mesomorphism.

title: Intramolecular electrophilic aminations of indoles enable divergent bond migrations to access piperidinoindolines and δ-carbolines
source: Physical sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: In contrast to well-established C–C migration rearrangements of spiro[indole-3,3’-pyrrolidine] systems, analogous transformations involving isomeric spiro[indole-3,2’-pyrrolidine] frameworks remain unexplored. Here, we demonstrate that unprotected spiro[indole-3,2’-pyrrolidine] intermediates can be generated via acid-catalyzed deprotection of indoles equipped with C3-tethered activated hydroxylamine units. Subsequent migration of the N-center from the C3 to the C2 position of the indolenine is followed by aerobic oxidation or trapping with electrophiles to yield piperidinoindolines. Notably, spiro[indole-3,2’-pyrrolidine] systems with an aryl substituent at C3’ undergo C–C migration in preference to C–N migration, leading to δ-carbolines. Related reactions employing indoles with C2-tethered aminating units are also presented. These strategies offer efficient and concise routes to synthetically challenging piperidinoindoline and δ-carboline scaffolds. The mechanisms of these new processes have been investigated experimentally and via density functional theory calculations. Furthermore, preliminary biological evaluation has revealed potent antitumor activity in selected derivatives.

title: 3D-printed Eutectic high-entropy alloys with dynamic protection for tribological damage resistance
source: Physical sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Maintaining the structural integrity of metallic materials under extreme localized shear poses a significant challenge for engineering reliability in the aerospace, automotive, and energy sectors, as such loading readily triggers catastrophic strain localization and surface delamination. Here, we report a nanoarchitecture-driven dynamic protection strategy to overcome this challenge. We engineer an FCC-dominant nanolamellar (FCC-NL) architecture in an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) by combining additive manufacturing (AM) with metastability engineering. Rather than undergoing the structural degradation observed in conventional EHEAs, this AM-enabled FCC-NL architecture orchestrates a robust hierarchical protective structure under severe sliding. It concurrently drives the bottom-up mechanochemical assembly of a damage-tolerant amorphous-nanocrystalline γ-Fe2O3 tribolayer and the top-down mechanical assembly of a strain-isolating nacre-like subsurface. This synergy yields a wear rate of 5.8 × 10−6 mm3 N−1 m−1, achieving an order-of-magnitude enhancement in surface damage resistance that surpasses currently reported values for bulk HEAs. This dynamic protection concept provides a design framework for developing highly surface-damage-tolerant alloys, essential to the reliability of critical engineering systems.

title: Architecture of the poxvirus early-transcription machinery and portal complex
abstract: Poxviruses enclose a complete viral transcription machinery alongside their dsDNA genome within the viral core, a transcription-competent compartment delimited by a permeable multi-layered protein shell. Upon infection of a cell and core release, this machinery almost immediately starts synthesizing early mRNAs, which are extruded across the core wall into the cytoplasm for translation. While in vitro structures of the isolated viral DNA-dependent RNA polymerase (vRNAP) have been described1–3, its native in virio architecture, spatial organization, and physical coupling to the genome remain unknown. Using cryo-electron tomography and sub-tomogram averaging on purified Vaccinia virus cores, we reveal that packaged vRNAP exists not as monomer, but as massive 1.8 MDa resting-state dimer bridged by fully ordered vaccinia virus early transcription factor (VETF). We also identify a subpopulation of these dimers bound to the essential kinase VPK2 and the core protein L4, which directly tether the transcribing engines to the packaged genome near the inner core wall. Furthermore, we determine a sub-nanometer structure of the putative poxvirus mRNA extrusion portal complex, revealing a rigid assembly integrated into the core wall comprising an E8 hexameric crown, an E6 hexameric central hub, and a basal L3 dodecameric channel suited for nucleic acid export. Together, these structures provide a comprehensive architectural blueprint of important components of the poxvirus core and open new structural and functional avenues for investigating poxvirus genome packaging, transcription activation, and mRNA extrusion.

title: Nanotechnology Meets Brain Diseases: Emerging Therapeutic Strategies for Drug Delivery
abstract: Abstract Brain diseases, encompassing neurodegenerative disorders, cerebrovascular diseases, and brain tumors, impose a profound global health burden. Conventional therapeutic strategies often fail due to the formidable blood–brain barrier (BBB) and complex pathological microenvironment of the central nervous system (CNS). The rapid evolution of nanotechnology offers unprecedented opportunities to overcome these delivery hurdles. This review comprehensively summarizes recent developments in engineered nanoplatforms for the diagnosis and targeted therapy of brain diseases. It first outlines the pathological characteristics and nanoprobe-enhanced diagnostic methods for various brain disorders, followed by a critical evaluation of five major classes of nanocarriers for CNS drug delivery: lipid-based, polymeric, inorganic, bio-derived, and hybrid nanocarriers. This evaluation highlights their structural attributes and delivery efficiencies. The discussion then examines advanced strategies to improve delivery precision, including multilevel targeting (e.g., BBB penetration and specific cell targeting), stimuli-responsive theranostics, and functional surface modifications. Linking these nanotechnological innovations to specific neurological diseases highlights their clinical potential. Finally, the review addresses current translational challenges, including biosafety, scalable manufacturing, and interindividual variability, and offers a forward-looking perspective on the rational design of next-generation precision neuro-nanomedicines.

title: Investigation of Structure‐Property‐Performance Relationships of Binders in Graphitic Negative Electrodes for Lithium Ion Batteries on the Example of Systematically Modified Xanthan
abstract: ABSTRACT This study investigates structure‐property‐performance relationships of xanthan‐based biopolymer binders in graphitic negative electrodes in lithium‐ion batteries. Xanthan gum (XG) variants possess well‐defined molecular structures and stable shear‐thinning behavior, which makes them ideal for systematic investigations. The influence of side chain composition, degree of acetylation and/or pyruvylation, and polymer molecular weight is investigated on electrode and paste properties (i.e., adhesion, conductivity, rheology, and electrochemical performance). A higher degree of acetylation enhances adhesion through improved interaction with the non‐polar copper current collector, while other properties remain unaffected. In contrast, a pyruvyl group reduces adhesion and conductivity due to poor compatibility with non‐polar components, promoting carbon‐binder heterogeneity. Larger side groups hinder adhesion and thixotropy (paste relaxation) as steric effects restrict polymer flexibility and prolong paste relaxation. Higher polymer molecular weight improves shear‐thinning behavior and thixotropy, minimizing sedimentation and edge effects, though slightly decreasing conductivity. Overall, these results establish clear correlations between the molecular structure of (XG‐based) biopolymer binders and electrode performance. The insights provide design guidelines for optimizing binder composition to balance rheological control, adhesion, and conductivity, contributing to more efficient electrode processing and improved performance in next‐generation lithium‐ion batteries.

title: Intrinsic Catalyst Reactivity—not Matched Surfactant Polarity—Drives Yield Differences in Aqueous Cross‐Coupling
abstract: ABSTRACT Micelles in aqueous–organic syntheses are commonly assumed to be the primary reaction sites that colocalize and transform reactants. However, under synthetically relevant high‐concentration conditions, including those used at scale in industrial pharmaceutical synthesis, phase separation may alter this simplified picture in poorly understood ways. Here, we investigate an aqueous Suzuki–Miyaura cross‐coupling producing a fluorescent product using triethylamine base and Kolliphor EL or Tween 80 surfactants. Fluorescence lifetime imaging microscopy (FLIM), dual‐channel imaging, and microspectroscopy reveal that micrometer‐scale triethylamine‐rich organic droplets, rather than nanoscale surfactant micelles, function as the predominant reaction sites. Direct measurements of droplet and micelle molecular compositions disprove a proposed product‐saturation inhibition mechanism based on surfactant polarity matching. Instead, the observed yield differences arise primarily from intrinsic catalyst reactivity. Surfactant‐free “on‐water” reactions further show that micelles are not required for productive coupling, supporting a primary role for surfactant in homogenization and mass transfer rather than creation of selective reaction compartments. This revised mechanistic assignment redirected reaction optimization from surfactant polarity to catalyst reactivity, affording 95% conversion to product in 20 min versus 26% under prior conditions. These findings challenge prevailing assumptions regarding micellar catalysis and demonstrate how microscale imaging can enable predictive optimization of aqueous reactions.

title: Synergistic Interface Lubrication and Anion Anchoring in a Composite Solid‐State Electrolyte for Dendrite‐Free and Wide‐Temperature Zinc Metal Batteries
abstract: ABSTRACT Solid‐state zinc‐ion batteries are promising for safe and flexible energy storage but suffer from low ionic conductivity and poor interfacial contact of polymer electrolytes. Herein, we report a composite solid‐state electrolyte (CSE) integrating 1‐ethyl‐3‐methylimidazolium bis(trifluoromethylsulfonyl)imide (EMIMTFSI) ionic liquid and boron nitride (BN) nanosheets into polyvinylidene fluoride hexafluoropropylene (PVDF‐HFP) matrix. EMIMTFSI acts as a plasticizer to suppress polymer crystallization, enhance ionic conductivity (5.23/0.76 mS cm −1 at 30/−20°C), and improve interfacial contact. Concurrently, BN anchors TFSI − via Lewis acid‐base interactions, regulating Zn 2+ −TFSI − coordination and facilitating ion dissociation, thereby guiding uniform Zn deposition along the (002) orientation. This synergy endows CSE with a high Zn 2+ transference number (0.56) and a low activation energy (0.21 eV). Consequently, Zn//Zn cell cycles stablely for 2000 h at 0.5 mAh cm −2 , and Zn//Cu cell delivers an average Coulombic efficiency of 99.75% for 1000 cycles. The Zn//hydrated aluminum vanadate (HAVO) full cell exhibits outstanding cycling stability (90.6% capacity retention after 6000 cycles), and stable operation at −20°C to 50°C. The Zn//HAVO pouch cell further demonstrates the practical viability of CSE in flexible electronics. This work presents a synergistic strategy for high‐performance polymer electrolytes, advancing the prospects of durable solid‐state zinc metal batteries.

title: 4 V‐Class Calcium‐Based Water‐in‐Salt Electrolyte for Aqueous Calcium‐Ion Batteries
abstract: ABSTRACT We report the first systematic investigation and demonstration of calcium bis(trifluoromethanesulfonyl)imide (Ca(TFSI) 2 ) as a water‐in‐salt electrolyte for aqueous calcium‐ion batteries (CIBs). At its solubility limit (6.2 m), Ca(TFSI) 2 exhibits a surprisingly wide electrochemical stability window (ESW) of 4.19 V, notably with the cathodic limit extending to ‐2.52 V vs Ag/AgCl, significantly surpassing previously reported Ca‐based aqueous electrolytes. Spectroscopic characterization combined with molecular simulations reveals a distinctive solvation structure in which Ca 2+ coordinates oxygen atoms from both H 2 O and TFSI − within the first coordination shell, with an average coordination number of 7. Extensive ion association is also evident through solvent‐shared ion pairs, consistent with suppressed water activity and an expanded ESW. Furthermore, the addition of a small amount of acetonitrile enables the electrolyte to remain liquid at sub‐zero temperatures, while lowering viscosity and enhancing ionic conductivity without substantially disrupting the Ca 2+ solvation structure. Leveraging these electrolyte properties, full cells employing perylene‐3,4,9,10‐tetracarboxylic diimide or Sn anodes and a Prussian blue analogue cathode demonstrate robust electrochemical performance at −20°C, including operation over a 3.2 V window with the Sn‐based cell, with long‐term cycling stability and sub‐zero device operation. These findings establish Ca(TFSI) 2 ‐based water‐in‐salt electrolytes as a versatile platform for wide‐voltage, low‐temperature aqueous CIBs.

title: Gating Oxygen Flux in High‐Nickel Layered Cathodes via a Surface‐Bulk Oxygen‐Fixation Framework
abstract: ABSTRACT High‐Ni layered oxide cathodes suffer from severe high‐voltage degradation driven by oxygen‐vacancy evolution, lattice oxygen release, and interfacial reconstruction. Here, a LaCeNb 6 O 18 ‐modified LiNi 0.867 Co 0.103 Mn 0.003 O 2 cathode is designed to establish an oxygen‐fixation‐gate (OFG) framework for regulating oxygen flux across the surface‐bulk region. The modified cathode establishes a spatial oxygen‐fixation‐gate framework, integrating bulk oxygen locking by Nb, surface oxygen retention by La/Ce, and interfacial oxygen buffering by the oxygen‐vacancy‐rich layer. STEM, depth‐resolved XPS, XAS, DEMS, EPR, in situ XRD, and DFT calculations reveal that this coupled regulation stabilizes both oxygen chemistry and structural evolution. Specifically, the oxygen‐vacancy formation energy at the fully delithiated state increases from 1.13 to 1.31 eV, O 2 evolution during initial high‐voltage charging is nearly eliminated, and oxygen‐defect accumulation during cycling is markedly restrained. Consequently, the optimized 867‐LCNO0.5 cathode delivers 158.15 mAh g −1 at 10 C, retains 87.23% capacity after 200 cycles, and maintains 80.03% retention after 200 cycles at 4.5 V vs. Li/Li + . This work establishes a spatially programmed oxygen‐fixation framework integrating bulk lattice oxygen locking, surface/subsurface oxygen anchoring, and interfacial oxygen‐vacancy buffering.

title: An artificial photoenzyme constrains substrates for selective antarafacial electrocyclizations
abstract:
Abstract
                  Electrocyclizations are a fundamental class of pericyclic transformations that can proceed through thermal or photochemical pathways. Although thermal electrocyclizations have been implicated in numerous biosynthetic pathways, there are few examples of enzyme-mediated processes, and the structural requirements for efficient catalysis are poorly understood. Here we develop an artificial photoenzyme for 6π-electrocyclizations (PhotoElectroCyclase PEC1.3) by introducing ten mutations into a recently reported [2 + 2]-cyclase. PEC1.3 processes diverse acrylanilide substrates with exceptional yields, regiocontrol and stereocontrol. A 1.3-Å crystal structure shows the substrate ideally positioned for energy transfer from a genetically programmed benzophenone triplet sensitizer. Interestingly, hydrogen-bonding interactions that were critical to [2 + 2] cyclase activity were abandoned during evolution of PEC1.3. Instead, the enzyme employs a network of hydrophobic interactions to constrain the substrate into a reactive geometry for selective antarafacial electrocyclization, allowing PEC1.3 to retain activity at cryogenic temperatures where appreciable molecular motions are frozen out. This example of controlled reaction outcomes without polar substrate–enzyme contacts points towards selective conversions of substrates lacking functional handles.

title: Photothermal-driven CO2 hydrogenation to methanol on an integrated Au–MoS2–TiO2 catalyst
abstract: Light-driven CO2 hydrogenation to methanol is constrained by insufficient broadband light utilization and inefficient CO2 activation. Herein, we achieve highly efficient photothermal hydrogenation of CO2 to methanol on an integrated Au–MoS2–TiO2 catalyst, in which MoS2 is anchored on TiO2 to form an intimate interface, and Au nanoparticles (NPs) are deposited on MoS2–TiO2. We demonstrate that the MoS2–TiO2 interface induces the formation of few-layered MoS2 and transfers electrons from TiO2 to MoS2. MoS2 serves as the primary active phase for CO2 hydrogenation, while Au NPs enhance photo-to-heat conversion via the localized surface plasmon resonance (LSPR) effect, thereby collectively facilitating CO2 activation under mild reaction conditions. Under photothermal conditions at 120°C in a continuous-flow reactor, the catalyst achieves 13.4% CO2 conversion with 84.7% methanol selectivity, and maintains stable performance over 400 hours without observable deactivation, underscoring it among the most competitive photothermal catalysts for CO2 hydrogenation to methanol.

title: Room temperature giant in-plane anomalous Hall effect in TbMn6Sn6
abstract: The anomalous Hall effect is the transverse voltage response in the presence of out-of-plane magnetization or non-zero Berry curvature, which, traditionally, is modulated by an out-of-plane magnetic field. Here we demonstrate a giant in-plane anomalous Hall effect (AHE) induced by coplanar magnetic fields in the quantum magnet TbMn6Sn6 at room temperature. The very large Hall conductivity arises in response to an applied in-plane magnetic field and results from the tilting of the ferrimagnetic axis of the Mn and Tb moments to the out of plane direction. With the in-plane magnetic field aligning the ferrimagnetic axis, the Berry curvature induced giant anomalous Hall effect is observed. Further, we show that the in-plane field induced AHE is more pronounced below the temperature induced spin reorientation, showing a 2π periodicity in angular dependent measurements. Unlike the in-plane Hall effect previously observed primarily at low temperatures, the AHE we observe here represents the largest room-temperature response reported in a single material. Our results reveal strong coupling between an in-plane magnetic field and out-of-plane Berry curvature, enabling new opportunities to engineer spintronic and quantum device responses at practical operating temperatures.

title: Injectable Self‐Healing Microspheres Enable In Situ Assembly of Dynamic Porous Scaffolds for Tissue Repair
abstract: ABSTRACT Tissue engineering scaffolds are indispensable for repairing complex tissue defects; however, conventional prefabricated scaffolds are limited by invasive implantation, poor anatomical conformity, and insufficient adaptability to irregular defect geometries. Here, we report an injectable, self‐assembling scaffold strategy that transforms polymer microspheres from isolated functional carriers into dynamic modular building blocks for in situ scaffold construction. Following injection, the self‐healing microspheres fill irregular defects, fuse with adjacent microspheres, and form a mechanically stable three‐dimensional scaffold with an interconnected porous architecture. This design combines the minimally invasive delivery and functional versatility of microspheres with the structural integrity and mechanical support of macroscopic scaffolds, thereby addressing a key challenge in precise and conformal tissue repair. The platform also enables disease‐specific functionalization through metal‐ion coordination. Silver‐ion‐loaded microspheres provide conformal coverage of complex wounds while exhibiting antibacterial activity and supporting skin regeneration. Zinc‐ion‐functionalized microspheres assemble into defect‐matched porous scaffolds and promote osteogenic repair. Copper‐ion‐integrated microspheres remain localized at tumor sites and provide sustained release of therapeutic agents, thereby reducing systemic toxicity. Collectively, this work establishes a minimally invasive, shape‐adaptive, and customizable scaffold platform for complex tissue repair and localized therapy. More broadly, it provides a versatile design framework for the development of next‐generation intelligent biomaterials.

title: Correction to “Soft Lithographic Patterning of Hyaluronic Acid on Hydrophilic Substrates Using Molding and Printing”
Anion‐Site Coupling Programs Interfacial Hydration for Electrocatalytic Hydrogenation
abstract: ABSTRACT Electrolyte anions are generally considered passive spectators at cathodically polarized interfaces, where electrostatic exclusion and strong solvation limit their access to catalytic sites. Here we establish anion‐site coupling as a strategy to program interfacial hydration and accelerate near‐neutral electrocatalytic hydrogenation. Molecularly defined Cu 2+ sites coordinated by hexahydroxytriphenylene on oxidized carbon black provide accessible coordination motifs that selectively couple with oxygen‐containing anions. Among HCO 3 − , CO 3 2− , and SO 4 2− , bicarbonate forms Cu 2+ ─HCO 3 − coupled sites that locally anchor water at the catalyst interface, replenishing otherwise depleted hydration regions and restoring hydrogen‐bond connectivity for proton transfer. This reconstructed hydration microenvironment accelerates proton‐coupled hydrogenation across chemically distinct substrates, enabling selective conversion of furfural to furfuryl alcohol, quinoline to tetrahydroquinoline, and nitrate to ammonia. In‐situ spectroscopy and theoretical analysis collectively reveal that anion coordination simultaneously restructures the local Cu coordination environment and interfacial water network, thereby lowering the kinetic barrier for proton‐coupled electron transfer. These findings establish coordinating anions as active molecular components of catalytic interfaces and introduce anion‐site coupling as a general strategy for programming interfacial hydration and proton‐transfer pathways in electrocatalytic synthesis.

title: Charge Escape Mechanism and Lifetime Prediction of Non‐Contact Triboelectric Sensors
abstract: ABSTRACT Non‐contact triboelectric sensors (NC‐TES) have attracted considerable attention for high‐frequency motion monitoring. However, their service life is fundamentally limited by the inevitable dissipation of surface charges. In this study, surface charges are categorized into retention and escape charges according to their escape behavior. Three charge escape mechanisms are systematically elucidated based on the electron trap energy distribution theory. On this basis, a general mathematical model is established to quantitatively characterize charge escape, enabling reliable prediction of the service life of NC‐TES. The influences of the intermediate layer, air gap of stator‐rotor, and humidity on the charge escape rate are investigated, providing design guidelines for improving sensor durability. Durability tests are performed on ten dielectric materials, among which fluorinated ethylene propylene (FEP) exhibits an expected lifetime of up to 8940 h at 100 Hz. Furthermore, the charge escape behavior of NC‐TES under various operating conditions is experimentally evaluated. The excellent agreement between the experimental results and theoretical predictions validates the proposed model, enabling accurate lifetime estimation and design optimization for specific operating conditions. This work establishes a theoretical framework for the design and lifetime prediction of NC‐TES, thereby facilitating the deployment of self‐powered sensing in industrial applications.

title: Tuning σ ‐Type Ni─O Orbital Hybridization for Stable Ultrahigh‐Ni Cathodes
abstract: ABSTRACT Ultrahigh‐Ni layered oxides have emerged as leading candidates for next‐generation high‐energy lithium‐ion batteries (LIBs), yet they suffer from severe chemo‐mechanical degradation driven by irreversible lattice oxygen loss during cycling. In this study, we propose an orbital hybridization regulation strategy via co‐doping high‐electronegativity cations (M = Zr 4+ /Ta 5+ /W 6+ ) to stabilize lattice oxygen and improve redox reversibility. Combined structural and theoretical analyses reveal that co‐doping induces electron redistribution around oxygen atoms, thereby weakening σ ‐type Ni–O hybridization and suppressing irreversible ligand‐to‐metal charge transfer and oxygen vacancy formation. Concurrently, the enhanced covalency of M─O bonds facilitates electron delocalization for charge compensation that reduces highly oxidized nickel species in the charged state. This stabilized redox chemistry mitigates transition metal (TM) migration, lattice distortion, and crack propagation. Additionally, elemental co‐doping also induces a lattice‐coherent rock‐salt surface layer that effectively suppresses interfacial parasitic reactions. The co‐doped cathode delivers exceptional cycling stability, with nearly 100% capacity retention after 100 cycles at 1 C (2.7–4.3 V) in half cells, and 93.5% retention after 500 cycles at 1 C (2.8–4.2 V) in pouch cells. This study provides an alternative avenue for stable ultrahigh‐Ni cathodes from the perspective of local chemistry and orbital hybridization modulation.

title: Reaction‐Pathway Regulation for Degradation‐Insensitive Direct Regeneration of Spent LiNi 0.5 Co 0.2 Mn 0.3 O 2 Cathode Materials
abstract: ABSTRACT Direct regeneration is limited by degradation‐dependent processing because cathodes with different degradation states cannot be regenerated using a uniform protocol. Using LiNi 0.5 Co 0.2 Mn 0.3 O 2 (NCM523) cathode materials with different degradation states, we show that this limitation originates from competition among relithiation, structural recovery, and thermal decomposition during calcination. As the balance of these competing reactions shifts with degradation state, cathodes evolve along distinct reaction trajectories. Recognizing that these reactions are governed by the reactants, we regulate the regeneration reaction through the lithium‐source reactant, causing cathode materials with different degradation states to pass through the same type of low‐symmetry, synthesis‐derived intermediate structure during calcination. This redirects regeneration toward a reconstruction pathway with favorable thermodynamics and improved ion diffusion, enabling rapid Li replenishment, long‐range cation ordering, and structural restoration. Consequently, practical NCM523 black mass is regenerated into cathodes that deliver higher capacity and better capacity retention than those regenerated via the conventional pathway, and a 1.3 Ah pouch cell with the regenerated cathode retains 80.2% of its initial capacity after 1000 cycles. This reconstruction pathway also enables direct upcycling of degraded NCM523 toward higher‐Ni compositions. Broadly, this work provides a mechanistic framework for reducing degradation‐state dependence in direct regeneration of spent cathode materials.

title: A Perspective on Hydrothermal Catalysis for Chemical Recycling of Polyolefin‐Rich Plastic Waste
abstract: ABSTRACT Polyolefins dominate global plastic production, yet most post‐consumer polyolefin waste is too mixed, wet, or contaminated for mechanical recycling. Hydrothermal liquefaction (HTL) converts such waste in hot, compressed water into hydrocarbon oils compatible with existing refineries and steam crackers, without pre‐drying. Water under hydrothermal conditions acts as a heat transfer medium, pseudo‐organic solvent, ionic catalyst, and purification phase, suppressing char and aromatics while partitioning heteroatoms into the aqueous phase. However, polyolefin degradation in hot water still proceeds through unselective radical scission, producing broad, waxy product distributions. This Perspective identifies catalysis as the key to achieving selective and scalable chemical recycling of polyolefins by HTL. Hydrothermal catalysis is distinct from catalytic pyrolysis, as water alters acid‐site chemistry, interfacial reactivity, and hydrogen availability while accelerating zeolite dealumination, support dissolution, and metal sintering. Catalyst design principles are discussed, including acid, metal, and bifunctional sites for selective chain scission and strategies for hydrothermal stability. Process integration of HTL oil with steam cracking, fluid catalytic cracking, and gasification is assessed, together with techno–economic and policy factors favoring olefins over fuels. Finally, research priorities are outlined, including long‐duration catalyst testing, mechanistic studies in hot compressed water, reactor scale‐up, and coupled techno–economic and life cycle assessment.

title: Enantioselective Coupling of 1,3‐Dienes and Vinyl Acetate for the Synthesis of Succinic Acids and β‐ and γ‐Amino Acids
abstract: ABSTRACT Catalyzed by cationic cobalt(I) complexes, [( L *)Co] + [X] − , 1,3‐dienes and vinyl carboxylates, two readily accessible electron‐rich class of substrates, undergo highly regio‐ and enantioselective heterodimerization giving skipped 1,4‐dienes with two configurationally defined, electronically differentiated double bonds flanking the newly formed stereogenic center (er typically >96:4). Among the numerous chelating bis ‐phosphine and phosphino‐oxazoline ligands, commercially available P ‐centered chiral ligand, (2 S , 2’ S , 3 S , 3’ S )‐MeO‐BIBOP incorporating a dibenzooxaphophole scaffold was found to be uniquely suited to give high yields and excellent regio‐ and enantioselectivities. Notably, in these additions, vinyl acetate serves as an acetaldehyde enolate surrogate. Configurations of the double bonds and of the stereogenic center were established by the crystal structure of the adduct from vinyl ester of ( S )‐naproxen and ( E )‐1,3‐nonadiene. The reaction has wide scope in both the 1,3‐dienes and a surprisingly broad array of highly functionalized vinyl esters, including vinyl sorbate, vinyl α ‐chloroacetate, vinyl methacrylate, vinyl α‐phenyl acrylate, and vinyl esters of α ‐amino acids. Functional groups, such as bromide, aldehyde, and vinyl groups, are tolerated in the vinyl esters. The coupling products carry multiple latent functionalities enabling their facile conversions to several useful classes of compounds, among them, chiral succinic acids, β‐ and γ‐amino acids, and 4‐alkyl γ‐butyrolactams.

title: Coupling Macrophage Reeducation With Mechanical Remodeling of the Tumor Extracellular Matrix to Enhance Pancreatic Cancer Immunotherapy
abstract: ABSTRACT One major challenge in reeducating macrophages lies in the specific delivery of therapeutic agents to these cells. Here we report a multi‐arm polymer conjugate of the toll‐like receptor 7/8 agonist resiquimod and soy protein (mPDPC‐RS) that simultaneously dismantles the immune and physical barriers within pancreatic tumors. Upon systemic administration, mPDPC‐RS preferentially accumulates in tumor‐associated macrophages in vivo, repolarizes them toward an antitumor phenotype, and thereby initiates robust immune responses. Concurrently, mPDPC‐RS reduces interstitial fluid pressure and solid stress of the tumor as well as tumor stiffness, thereby facilitating CD8 + T cell infiltration. In murine pancreatic cancer models, this dual‐function platform produces profound tumor suppression and markedly extends survival. Our findings provide a versatile platform with high macrophage avidity for cancer immunotherapy and establish a comprehensive strategy for overcoming both biological and mechanical defenses of the tumor microenvironment to improve immunotherapeutic outcomes in pancreatic cancer.

title: Steric Asymmetry‐Induced Hyperconjugation Enables Stable Anode‐Free Sodium Pouch Cells
abstract: ABSTRACT Anode‐free sodium batteries (AFSBs) hold great promise for high‐energy storage; however, their practical application is hindered by poor cycling stability arising from inefficient sodium‐metal electroplating–stripping. Guided by hyperconjugation theory, 1‐ethoxy‐2‐methoxyethane (EEME) is identified as the optimal solvent, as its sterically asymmetric ethyl terminus provides a hyperconjugation‐enabled polarization pathway while maintaining moderate Na + ‐coordination strength. This steric‐induced hyperconjugation amplifies the positive electrostatic potential in EEME, creating a persistent anion‐affinitive site that retains PF 6 − near Na + solvation structures and promotes their correlated transport toward the negatively polarized electrode. The resulting NaF‐rich interphase enables highly reversible and dendrite‐free Na electroplating/stripping. Benefiting from these, at pouch‐cell level, the EEME‐based electrolyte enabled durable anode‐free Al/C||Na 4 Fe 3 (PO 4 ) 2 P 2 O 7 cells, retaining remarkable 85.9% after 1600 cycles at 0.5C with superior rate capability up to 5C. Notably, the EEME‐based electrolyte also enabled excellent low‐temperature performance, with the pouch cell preserving 98.6% of its room‐temperature capacity at −20 °C and retaining 93.5% capacity after 150 cycles. This work establishes the stereoelectronic‐solvation design principle that connects fundamental conformational chemistry with rational electrolyte engineering for practical AFSBs.

title: Designing solar panels for realistic end-of-life scenarios
abstract: The rapid growth of photovoltaics is generating vast waste streams, a portion of which flows to regions where recycling is unregulated. Solar panel design criteria do not account for these end-of-life realities, creating global asymmetry in environmental burdens. This Comment proposes research directions beyond material substitution to address these design gaps.

title: Size‐Dependent Photoelectric and Photothermal Effects in Plasmon‐Induced Hydrogen Evolution Reaction
abstract: ABSTRACT Plasmonic photocatalysis relies on the conversion of photon energy into nonequilibrium charge carriers and heat. However, the relative contributions of these processes and their size‐dependent roles in photocatalysis remain unclear because of their intrinsically intertwined nature. Here, size‐controlled Ag NPs/p‐GaN heterostructures are employed to quantitatively disentangle the size‐dependent roles of hot‐electron injection and surface heating in determining photocatalytic activity. title: Multiscale Engineering of Three‐Phase Interfaces for Proton Exchange Membrane Fuel Cells
abstract: ABSTRACT Proton exchange membrane fuel cells (PEMFCs) offer high efficiency and zero‐emission operation, yet membrane electrode assembly performance is constrained by coupled oxygen, proton, electron, and water transport. This review summarizes advances in multiscale three‐phase interface engineering. At the nanoscale, catalyst protection, catalyst–ionomer interactions, molecular modifiers, and ionomer design improve active site accessibility and oxygen transport. At the electrode scale, support microenvironments and catalyst layer architectures regulate pore connectivity, wettability, ionomer distribution, electronic conduction, and water removal. At the device scale, structured assemblies, membranes, gas diffusion layers, microporous layers, and flow fields coordinate mass and charge transport under practical conditions. Future priorities include scalable fabrication, operando diagnostics, multiscale modeling, and AI‐assisted optimization. By integrating interfacial, electrode, and device engineering, this review provides a framework for developing durable, high‐power, low‐platinum PEMFCs and advancing automotive fuel cell stacks with improved performance, lifetime, and economic feasibility.

title: Nanocatalytic modulation of thrombin-ferroptosis axis for efficient intervention of ischemic stroke
abstract: Ischemic stroke represents a leading cause of global mortality. Current therapeutic strategies, including recombinant tissue plasminogen activator and mechanical thrombectomy, are constrained by suboptimal recanalization, high recurrence rates, and reperfusion injury. In this work, we initially identified elevated intrathrombotic thrombin as a critical mediator of fibrinolytic resistance and a driver of ferroptosis-related neuronal injury following stroke. To specifically target this thrombin dysregulation, we designed ultrasmall tungsten-based polyoxometalate (W-POM) nanodots capable of penetrating the blood-brain barrier. In addition to their specific reactive oxygen species-scavenging capability, W-POM nanodots primarily modulate thrombin activity and attenuate its pathological signaling. In both thrombin-induced and ischemia-reperfusion injury models, W-POM nanodots significantly improve neurological outcomes by directly suppressing thrombin activity and inhibiting thrombin-driven ferroptosis. Furthermore, W-POM nanodots remodel the thrombotic microenvironment and reduce neuroinflammation, thereby conferring robust neuroprotection. This study highlights the thrombin-ferroptosis pathway as a key mechanistic axis in stroke and introduces a nanotherapeutic platform for targeted thrombin modulation in ischemic stroke therapy.

title: Dual‐Asymmetric Giant Molecule Acceptors Featuring Asymmetric Terminals and Flexible Alkyl‐Flank Architecture for Efficient and Robust Non‐Halogen Solvent‐Processed Binary and Ternary Organic Solar Cells
abstract: ABSTRACT Flexible‐linked giant‐molecule acceptors (F‐GMAs) suffer from inferior intermolecular packing, limiting their efficiency in non‐halogenated processed binary organic solar cells (OSCs). Moreover, asymmetric‐terminal‐based regioregular F‐GMAs remain challenging. Here, we propose a dual‐asymmetric‐rigid‐within‐flexible molecular strategy and synthesize four flanking linker‐based F‐GMAs ( DY4T‐F , DY8T‐F , DY12T‐F , dual‐asymmetric ADY8T‐FCl ) by progressively lengthening the alkyl linker and symmetric/asymmetric terminals, alongside a dual‐asymmetric monomeric AY4T‐FCl . The AY4T‐FCl crystal exhibited diverse intermolecular packing modes and efficient charge transport channels due to the synergistic outer thienyl flanking chain and asymmetric terminals. ADY8T‐FCl exhibits stronger intramolecular folding, enhanced crystallinity, and higher electron mobility than other neat films. o ‐XY: CS 2 ‐processed D18 : ADY8T‐FCl ‐based as‐cast binary OSCs yield a remarkable PCE of 20.35% with a low nonradiative recombination energy loss (Δ E 3 ) of 0.183 eV, setting benchmarks for all‐F‐GMA‐based and non‐halogenated‐solvent‐processed binary OSCs. Notably, D18 : ADY8T‐FCl flexible binary OSCs achieve an outstanding PCE of 18.41%, significantly better than other counterparts. More interestingly, D18 : L8‐BO‐X : ADY8T‐FCl ‐based devices achieve a champion PCE of 20.82% among F‐GMAs‐based ternary OSCs. Our work demonstrates that the dual‐asymmetric‐rigid‐within‐flexible strategy for flank‐connected F‐GMAs with alkyl‐length engineering and asymmetric terminals offers a promising pathway for concurrently achieving record efficiency, ultralow Δ E 3 , and superior mechanical robustness in non‐halogenated processed flexible/rigid binary and rigid ternary OSCs.

title: Nucleophile–electrophile chemistry produces a stable interphase for long-Life anode-Less lithium metal batteries
abstract: Anode-less lithium (Li) metal batteries (ALLMBs) represent the optimal cell architecture for maximizing energy density, yet their practical viability is severely hindered by poor cycling life. This limitation stems from the unstable solid-electrolyte interphase (SEI), which drives continuous parasitic reactions with Li metal and induces severe interfacial degradation. Here we report a nucleophile–electrophile bridging strategy to construct a robust, passivating SEI that enables long-term stable cycling of ALLMBs. By leveraging a nucleophilic substitution mechanism, electron-rich organic species derived from the solvent, acting as nucleophiles, are covalently bridged by electron-deficient, boron-centred electrophiles derived from the anion. This molecular-level integration overcomes the inherent fragility of the SEI organic phase, generating mechanically robust oligoborates that resist interfacial degradation, along with lithium fluoride (LiF) nanocrystals nucleated in-situ to facilitate rapid Li+ transport. The resulting oligoborate–LiF hybrid SEI enables highly reversible Li plating/stripping and remarkably extends the ALLMB cycling life by 12-fold, maintaining 80% capacity over 300 cycles. The superior cyclability is maintained even under stringent practical conditions (high cathode loading, lean electrolyte supply, and pouch-cell operation). This work establishes a fundamentally new paradigm in interphase engineering, paving the way for high-energy, reliable ALLMBs.

title: Dithioerythritol Enables Synchronized Crystallization and Buried Interface Passivation for Sn–Pb Perovskite Tandems
abstract: ABSTRACT Tin‐lead (Sn‐Pb) mixed narrow‐bandgap (NBG) perovskites (PVK) are key to all‐perovskite tandem solar cells (AP‐TSCs), but their development is hindered by Sn 2+ oxidation and mismatched crystallization kinetics between Sn and Pb species. A critical issue is the “skin effect” during film formation, which traps solvent at the buried interface, creating voids and undercoordinated defects that cause non‐radiative recombination. Here, we introduce dithioerythritol (DTE) as a multifunctional additive. DTE's bidentate thiol groups coordinate with both Pb 2+ and Sn 2+ , inducing delayed nucleation and slow growth, allowing complete solvent escape and eliminating voids. Simultaneously, DTE passivates defects, suppresses Sn 2+ oxidation, and optimizes interfacial energy alignment. Consequently, DTE‐treated films show enhanced crystallinity, no buried voids, reduced Sn 4+ fraction (from 50.27% to 22.95%), 50% lower trap density, and 7.9‐fold longer carrier lifetime. The optimized single‐junction NBG cell achieves 23.31% efficiency (Reverse scan, RS) with damp heat (DH) stability T 80 of 750 h, outperforming the control (20.50%, 320 h). When integrated into monolithic two‐terminal (2T) tandems, the champion device delivers 28.82% efficiency (RS) and DH stability T 80 of 1290 h, a 2.5‐fold enhancement over the control. This work demonstrates DTE as a promising additive that synchronizes crystallization, passivates defects, suppresses oxidation, and optimizes electronic structure for efficient and stable AP‐TSCs.

title: Hierarchically Porous Unsubstituted Olefin‐Linked COF With Synergistically Enhanced Electronic and Ionic Conductivities for High‐Performance Lithium‐Ion Battery Cathodes
abstract: ABSTRACT The development of covalent organic frameworks (COFs) with synergistically enhanced ionic/electronic conductivities, improved active site utilization, and increased chemical stability for achieving high‐performance lithium–ion battery (LIB) cathodes remain a significant challenge. Here, we report the rational design of a novel unsubstituted olefin–linked, highly crystalline COF (namely HATN–ICTO COF) as a cathode for LIBs. The HATN–ICTO COF integrates extended fully conjugated π–networks, hierarchical porosity, and dual redox–active centers, enabling a synergistic improvement in ionic and electronic conductivity as well as a high theoretical capacity. This unique unsubstituted olefin linkage also endows the COF with excellent chemical stability, thereby ensuring long‐term cycling performance. Meanwhile, the hierarchical porous architecture of the COF can effectively buffer the volume expansion during repeated charge–discharge processes, mitigating electrode damage. The COF delivers a high specific capacity of 293 mAh g − 1 at 0.1 A g − 1 and maintains 206 mAh g − 1 at 10.0 A g − 1 , with outstanding cycling performance of 155 mAh g − 1 at 5.0 A g − 1 after 18,000 cycles. Additionally, a pouch cell based on the HATN–ICTO COF//Li configuration was also demonstrated. This work provides fundamental insights into structure–property relationships governing charge delocalization and redox activity in COFs.

title: Spin and Charge Engineering of a BiCuMn Nanoalloy Catalyst for Industrial‐Scale Electrosynthesis of Glycine
abstract: ABSTRACT Electrocatalytic C–N coupling provides a sustainable route for α‐amino acids, yet its practicality is limited by poor selectivity and durability at industrially relevant current densities. Here, we report a Bi‐based nanoalloy catalyst with atomically dispersed Cu and Mn (BiCuMn@C) for industrial‐level glycine electrosynthesis. Experimental and theoretical results reveal that Cu modulates the electronic structure of Bi sites via d ‐ p hybridization, enhancing the adsorption/activation of nitrogen‐containing species, while spin‐polarized electrons from Mn are delivered to adjacent *NO intermediates, promoting their hydrogenation to *NHO on the pathway to NH 2 OH. This spin‐charge engineering disrupts the intrinsic scaling relationship between *NO and *NHO adsorption, enabling simultaneous enhancement of activity and selectivity. As a result, BiCuMn@C achieves a glycine Faradaic efficiency of 78.9% at a current density of 533.1 mA cm −2 , corresponding to a yield rate of 1569 µmol h −1 cm −2 , and extends to the efficient synthesis of five additional amino acids. In a membrane‐electrode assembly (MEA) electrolyzer, the catalyst sustains stable operation for over 1000 h with a cumulative glycine production exceeding 1 mol. This work achieves one of the best overall performances reported to date and provides practical design guidance for the industrially relevant electrosynthesis of α‐amino acids.

title: Function‐Decoupled Dual‐Anion Doping via Site‐Preferential Regulation Enables High‐Performance Lithium Argyrodite Electrolytes
abstract: ABSTRACT All‐solid‐state lithium metal batteries adopting argyrodite‐type sulfide solid‐state electrolytes (SSEs) offer enhanced safety and energy density, yet face challenges in balancing ionic conductivity, air stability and interfacial compatibility. Herein, we pioneer a precursor‐directed site‐preferential dual‐anion doping strategy to address these trade‐offs. Density functional theory (DFT) calculations reveal the oxygen precursor dictates the predominant anion occupancy: Li 2 O kinetically favors O at the 4d sites, whereas P 2 O 5 preferentially directs O to the 16e sites. Guided by this principle, Li 6 PS 4.2 O 0.4 Se 0.4 Cl (LPSOSeCl) SSEs is designed, wherein O preferentially enriches 16e sites to enhance air stability and widen the electrochemical window for high‐voltage cathode compatibility, whereas Se preferentially enriches 4d sites to compensate ionic conductivity and promote a Li 2 Se/Li 2 O‐rich interphase for dendrite suppression. Ab initio molecular dynamics (AIMD) simulations combined with radial distribution functions (RDFs) further reveal that the Se/O co‐doping facilitates the formation of a stable Li/SSE interface, significantly inhibiting LPSOSeCl SSE reduction. The resulting LPSOSeCl SSE achieves high ionic conductivity, excellent moist air stability and remarkable critical current density (CCD) of 2.6 mA cm −2 . The Li||Li symmetric cells demonstrate ultralong cycling stability over 4000 h at 0.2 mA cm −2 and LiNi 0.8 Co 0.1 Mn 0.1 O 2 full cells rentain 70.7% capacity retention after 500 cycles at 0.3C.

title: Aqueous π‐Hole Interactions Enabled by Chiral Perfluoroarene Amphiphiles
abstract: ABSTRACT Arene‐perfluoroarene (AP) interactions, as a representative class of π‐hole‐driven noncovalent interactions, have demonstrated unique advantages in molecular recognition and supramolecular assembly. However, the precise regulation of hydrophobic aromatic molecules in aqueous environments through AP interactions remains challenging. Herein, we designed and constructed a series of chiral perfluoroarene amphiphiles based on an octafluoronaphthalene scaffold, in which the amphiphilicity, self‐assembly behavior, and confined microenvironment were regulated through end‐group engineering, enabling selective recognition and photophysical modulation of polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs). These perfluoroarene amphiphiles readily formed stable lamellar vesicular assemblies in aqueous solution. The π‐hole region of the perfluoroarene moiety interacted with PAHs through AP interactions, facilitating the incorporation of guest molecules into the confined lamellar domains. Consequently, a variety of hydrophobic PAHs were successfully encapsulated in aqueous media, accompanied by effective modulation of their excited‐state behaviors. Moreover, the chiral confined microenvironment induced chiroptical responses from achiral PAHs, enabling efficient chirality transfer. This work provides a new design strategy for aqueous supramolecular recognition, aromatic guest aggregation regulation, and the construction of chiral photofunctional materials based on AP interactions.

title: Continuous N-to-C Peptide Synthesis
abstract: Current state-of-the-art peptide synthesis faces a significant global challenge in efficiency and sustainability.1 With demand for peptide therapeutics growing rapidly,2,3 our ability to provide these important medicines is under increasing pressure.4 Chemical synthesis typically proceeds C-to-N and requires protecting groups, whereas ribosomal synthesis proceeds N-to-C from unprotected amino acids (AAs). To improve efficiency and sustainability, we developed a continuous N-to-C Peptide Synthesis (NCPS) using N-/C-unprotected AAs or fragments without intermediate isolations, achieving ≥95% average yield per coupling and ≤1.0% epimerization. The method enabled seven consecutive couplings. Starting from N-/C-unprotected AAs, peptide assembly requires fewer isolations than those needed to prepare the corresponding Fmoc-AA building blocks before conventional synthesis can begin. This method accepts all 20 canonical AAs and a wide range of non-canonical AAs important for drug-like profiles.5 Longer peptides can be readily assembled through continuous fragment coupling while maintaining chiral integrity. This approach reduces isolations by ~10-fold and waste generation by up to ~100-fold. We further developed a flow synthesizer that enhances speed and productivity while mitigating batch manufacturing risks. The method enabled the synthesis of a tirzepatide heptapeptide fragment, degarelix, a 14-mer engineered macrocyclic peptide, and semaglutide. Overall, continuous NCPS has the potential to transform peptide manufacturing.

title: Active Site Migration in Heterogeneous Hydrogenation by Coupling N‐Doped Carbon and Platinum
abstract: ABSTRACT In heterogeneous hydrogenation, porous carbon supports are usually treated as passive dispersants or electronic scaffolds for metal nanoparticles. Here, we show that in specifically designed N‐doped carbon electrically coupled to Pt, the operative reduction locus can shift between catalyst components. Using p‐nitrophenol (pNP) hydrogenation as a model reaction, we decouple hydrogen activation from substrate reduction in unbiased electrochemical and thermochemical configurations. While Pt/C is required for hydrogen activation, the nitrogen‐doped TCNQ900 carbon acts as an efficient pNP reduction interface once supplied with ‐derived electrons and protons. Electrochemical measurements show that coupling to TCNQ900 displaces Pt/C from its / equilibrium along its hydrogen oxidation polarization curve, establishing a mixed‐potential‐driven electron flux toward the carbon phase. Under high ‐activation capacity, Pt‐centered (thermochemical) and carbon‐centered reductions (electrochemical) operate in parallel, increasing the overall rate. Under ‐activation‐limited conditions, electrical coupling relocates the dominant reduction locus from Pt/C to TCNQ900 with little change in total rate. We describe this reversible redistribution of catalytic function as active‐site migration. These results show that carbons can be chemically designed to serve not as passive supports, but as electronically coupled reduction interfaces that redirect hydrogenation pathways in multicomponent catalysts.
